newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-North American Q3 paper profits to plunge.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-North American Q3 paper profits to plunge.

text.p: North American pulp, paper and forest products companies are set to report sharply lower third-quarter profits due to slumping prices, high inventories and slackening demand, analysts said.

A survey of analysts' third-quarter earnings estimates for 47 U.S. and Canadian forest products companies by I.B.E.S International showed aggregate earnings falling by 57 percent to US$1.1 billion in the latest quarter from US$2.8 billion a year earlier.

While earnings for makers of paper and consumer products will be hurt, profits for producers of key commodities such as pulp and newsprint could tumble up to 100 percent from a year earlier, analysts said.
"Three things will cause a decrease from the third-quarter results -- lower prices, higher costs and lower volumes," said Don Roberts of CIBC Wood Gundy Inc.
"The only good news out there, which is already in the market, is lumber, and people are looking at a bottoming out of the other commodities," he said.

Pulp prices are down 40 percent from last year's third quarter, while linerboard is off 38 percent and white papers have slipped 25 percent. Newsprint prices have declined at least 25 percent from March 1996.
In Canada, most of the big pulp and paper commodity producers such as Abitibi-Price Inc, Noranda Forest Inc and Avenor Inc are expected to show sharply lower third-quarter earnings.
But smaller lumber producers such as West Fraser Timber Co, Donohue Inc, Uniforet Inc and Groupe Forex Inc should report fairly solid earnings.

In the United States, two companies that already reported lower third-quarter numbers, Champion International Corp and International Paper Co, beat analysts' consensus estimates, boosted partly by their timber operations.
George Adler, of Smith Barney Research, said the third quarter was "a disaster" for the paper and forest products sector.
"The U.S. paper industry is in recession and in Canada. The newsprint industry is even worse," he said.
The profit decline will likely extend to the fourth quarter, depending on the sector, analysts said.

Adler said the pulp and paper industry's problems began in 1994/95 when production surged as commodity prices soared and customers were aggressively accumulating inventory. By autumn 1995, prices began falling, except for newsprint, which began its decline last spring.

A recent pulp price increase appears to be sticking, but some analysted predict another fallback. A hike in linerboard/corrugated boxes prices planned for October seems shaky -- worrisome news for the American producers gearing up for the busy Christmas season.
"Linerboard and corrugated are as important to the U.S. industry as newsprint is to the Canadian industry," Adler said.
In Canada, inventory reductions in newsprint will hurt the sector and could muddy fourth-quarter earnings with inventory writedowns.

Note: Estimates are consensus mean. Negative figures denote loss.
